studio.name: Aariv's Web Studio
studio.tagline: Fast, accessible, zero-dependency static websites built pro bono for local animal rescues and food pantries.
studio.intro: I'm Aariv, a high-school freshman. I started this small studio after noticing that local volunteer-run charities either had broken WordPress themes from 2014 or slow page-builder sites that buried basic answers like 'When is the pantry open?' or 'How do I foster a cat?' beneath 4 MB of JavaScript. Every site here is built for free, ships as hand-crafted static HTML & CSS with zero runtime dependencies, passes strict WCAG AA/AAA contrast checks, and loads in under half a second on a budget phone.

sites.name: A foster-based cat rescue
sites.kind: Charity website · Free build · Mobile-first adoption & foster funnel
sites.summary: A warm, phone-first site for an all-volunteer foster cat network. Designed around the reality that 82% of their visitors arrive from Instagram or Facebook links on a phone and decide within ten seconds whether to apply to foster, browse cats, or donate.
sites.what: Foster-based cat rescue: mission, adoptable cats, foster onboarding checklist, and recurring donor pathways. Built to load fast and read warmly on a phone, since most adopters and donors arrive from social links.
sites.audience: Prospective fosters and adopters browsing from mobile social feeds, often during a commute or evening scroll.
sites.problemStatement: Because the rescue doesn't have a physical shelter building, visitors kept asking where they could 'visit the cats' and dropping off before reading how foster-to-adopt works. Their old link-tree style page split donations, foster applications, and cat bios across four mismatched third-party forms.
sites.whatIBuilt: I designed an editorial card layout that explains the 3-step foster-to-adopt loop right below the hero before showing the adoptable cat grid. Each cat card uses explicit width/height attributes to eliminate layout shift (CLS = 0.00) and badges medical/temperament tags ('Good with dogs', 'Bonded pair', 'FIV+') in plain text rather than tiny icons.
sites.whatWasTricky: Volunteer coordinators needed to update cat availability without touching layout code, and foster photos come in every aspect ratio imaginable. I built a CSS aspect-ratio frame (`4 / 3` with `object-fit: cover` and focal-point utility classes) plus a clean JSON-to-HTML card partial so cropping never decapitates ear tips or distorts portraits.
accessibilityNotes: Every adoptable cat card uses a single composite link with an explicit `aria-label` ('Meet Mochi - 2-year-old tabby, good with other cats') instead of three redundant 'Learn More' buttons.
Warm cream canvas (`#FBF8F3`) paired with deep espresso ink (`#1F1A17`) hits 14.8:1 contrast, easy on the eyes without sterile pure-white glare.
Donation tier buttons work as native radio labels with full keyboard arrow navigation and 52px height on mobile.

typography.monoFont: SF Mono / ui-monospace (13px tabular-nums for medical tags & stats)

gridSpec.mobile: Single-column stack (375px), sticky bottom 'Foster / Donate' bar with 52px tap targets, 16px outer gutter.
gridSpec.tablet: 2-column adoptable cat grid (768px), 24px gap, inline step-by-step foster timeline.
gridSpec.desktop: 12-column Swiss editorial grid (max-width 1160px), 3-column cat roster + asymmetric 5/7 split hero.

sites.name: A community food pantry
sites.kind: Charity website · Free build · Zero-stigma emergency food access
sites.summary: Built for neighbors looking up distribution hours, bus routes, and eligibility rules, often on a prepaid phone with spotty data while standing outside or riding transit. Clarity, dignity, and large type come before everything else.
sites.what: Free-food pantry: hours, location, what to expect on a first visit. Plain language and large type, because visitors are often in a hurry or stressed.
sites.audience: Neighbors seeking groceries for their household, plus community volunteers checking shift times and most-needed shelf-stable donations.
sites.problemStatement: On too many food pantry sites, the distribution hours are trapped inside a scanned PDF flyer or buried below a 600-word mission statement for donors. If someone is stressed and trying to find out whether they need a photo ID or utility bill before the pantry closes at 6 PM, making them pinch-zoom a PDF is a design failure.
sites.whatIBuilt: I put the live weekly schedule, street address, transit directions, and a bold 'No ID or proof of income required, everyone is welcome' banner in the top 320 pixels of the viewport. Right underneath is a four-step 'What happens on your first visit' walkthrough written at a 6th-grade reading level so first-time visitors know where to park, that volunteers provide boxes, and that they get to choose their own groceries.
sites.whatWasTricky: The pantry serves two completely different audiences: neighbors picking up food (who need hours and zero friction) and donors/volunteers (who need drop-off windows and a list of high-priority pantry staples like cooking oil and canned protein). I separated the two flows right in the top bar so donor fundraising appeals never get in the way of someone looking for food.
accessibilityNotes: Base body font size is 18px with 1.65 line-height; schedule tables use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` and never scroll horizontally at 320px.
Zero-stigma language review: removed bureaucratic terms like 'beneficiaries' and 'intake verification' in favor of 'neighbors' and 'first visit'.
High-contrast forest green (`#183A2C`) on warm alabaster (`#F9F8F4`) achieves 12.1:1 contrast for outdoor afternoon readability.

typography.headingFont: Public Sans / System UI, sans-serif (800, tight -0.025em)
typography.monoFont: SF Mono / ui-monospace (14px for hours, bus numbers & zip codes)

gridSpec.mobile: 1-column priority stack (375px): Open Hours card first, First-Visit guide second, Needed Items third.
gridSpec.tablet: 2-column asymmetric split (768px): Schedule + Map card pinned left, First-Visit FAQ right.
gridSpec.desktop: 12-column Swiss utility grid (max-width 1140px) with 2px solid structural dividers and print-friendly stylesheet.

sites.name: A no-kill cat rescue
sites.kind: Charity website · Free build · High-trust medical fund & adoption showcase
sites.summary: No-kill rescues take in senior, diabetic, and injured cats that municipal shelters can't treat, which means vet bills are their biggest bottleneck. I designed this site around big, honest portrait photography and a persistent, transparent medical-fund donation path.
sites.what: No-kill cat rescue: adoptable cats, foster program and donate flow. Designed around big friendly photography and a sticky donate path, since rescue sites live or die on donations.
sites.audience: Recurring monthly donors, local cat adopters, and clinic sponsors checking how medical donations are spent.
sites.problemStatement: Donors are much more generous when they know what their money actually buys ($25 covers microchip + rabies vaccine; $120 covers a dental extraction), but the rescue's old site only had a generic PayPal button buried in the footer. Meanwhile, special-needs and senior cats sat at the bottom of the page with tiny thumbnails.
sites.whatIBuilt: I created a sticky header donate trigger paired with concrete 'What your gift covers' cost-breakdown cards ($25, $50, $120, $250) and a spotlight rail for senior and bonded-pair cats. The photography grid uses progressive responsive image sizing so full-bleed cat portraits look crisp on Retina displays while staying under a strict 16 KB HTML+CSS budget.
sites.whatWasTricky: Sticky donate bars on phones can easily feel pushy or cover up content when someone is trying to read a cat's medical bio. I tuned the mobile bar to sit cleanly in the top header with a compact pill button (`min-height: 44px`) and built the cost-breakdown cards using pure CSS grid so nothing overlaps or janks during scroll.
accessibilityNotes: Every donation amount card exposes its full description to screen readers ('Donate $50 - covers initial bloodwork and FIV/FeLV test for one intake').
No auto-playing carousels or background video: all cat spotlights sit in a keyboard-focusable static grid.
Tested with macOS VoiceOver and Safari Reader mode to ensure every cat's age, spay/neuter status, and adoption fee reads in logical DOM order.

typography.headingFont: Instrument Serif / Baskerville, serif (600, warm editorial display)
typography.monoFont: SF Mono / ui-monospace (13px for dollar impact tiers & intake IDs)

gridSpec.mobile: 1-column portrait cards (375px), 2×2 donation impact tier grid, persistent top donate button.
gridSpec.tablet: 2-column featured senior cats + 4-column impact tier strip (768px).
gridSpec.desktop: 12-column editorial layout (max-width 1180px) with 7/5 hero split and 3-column adoption gallery.

sites.name: A community-cat (TNR) rescue
sites.kind: Charity website · Free build · Field manual for colony caretakers
sites.summary: When someone finds a litter of outdoor cats behind their apartment or workplace, they don't want cute animations, they need to know whether the kittens are old enough to trap, how to borrow a humane box trap, and which clinic takes ear-tip appointments tomorrow morning.
sites.what: Community-cat rescue (trap, neuter, return): explains TNR in plain language with a step-by-step for first-time colony caretakers. Information-first design; the audience needs answers, not animations.
sites.audience: First-time neighborhood colony caretakers, property managers, and trap-loan volunteers working out in the field at dawn or dusk.
sites.problemStatement: TNR (Trap-Neuter-Return) has strict timing rules: you have to withhold food 24 hours before trapping, line the trap with newspaper, cover it with a breathable sheet to calm the cat, and never trap nursing mothers without locating the kittens. Previously, volunteers were texting paragraphs of instructions over SMS at 11 PM because the website didn't have a clear checklist.
sites.whatIBuilt: I structured the entire homepage like a rugged field manual: a numbered 5-step TNR timeline ('1. Assess & Count → 2. Book Clinic Spot → 3. Trap Loan & Bait → 4. Spay/Neuter + Ear Tip → 5. Recovery & Return'), a visual 'Found Kittens? Wait Before You Scoop' age decision tree, and a trap-loan request block that works on old browsers without a single line of client JS.
sites.whatWasTricky: TNR instructions are dense, and long walls of text cause people to miss critical safety steps (like keeping traps indoors overnight after anesthesia so cats can regulate their body temperature). I used Swiss-grid callout boxes with high-contrast warning stripes (`Warning: Post-Op Temperature Rule`) and semantic `<details>` accordions so caretakers can scan the 5 steps in 15 seconds or expand the exact step they're standing in front of.
accessibilityNotes: Native HTML `<details>` and `<summary>` elements power the field-checklist expanders, 100% keyboard and screen-reader accessible with 0 KB of JavaScript.
Ear-tip identification diagram includes full prose alt text explaining the universal 3/8-inch straight left-ear tip.
High-visibility slate and ochre field palette tested at 14.9:1 primary contrast for reading under streetlights or bright sun.

typography.headingFont: Space Grotesk / System UI, sans-serif (700, technical manual clarity)
typography.monoFont: SF Mono / ui-monospace (13.5px for step numbers, weights & clinic hours)

gridSpec.mobile: 1-column numbered field checklist (375px), large step badges, tap-to-expand native `<details>` drawers.
gridSpec.tablet: 2-column decision tree ('Friendly Stray' vs 'Unsocialized Community Cat') at 768px.
gridSpec.desktop: 12-column Swiss specification grid (max-width 1160px) with sticky left step index and printable trap-loan checklist.
